title: Keep the Batch Running After Logout
description:
**SITUATION:**

Every night someone runs `/opt/order-processor/bin/batch-export` by hand to push the day's orders to the warehouse. The run takes about an hour. Twice this week the export died halfway because the engineer's laptop went to sleep and the terminal closed. The warehouse got only half the orders.

The binary is already on the box. You start it yourself. Until this export is turned into a proper service, it has to keep running after you log out: the process must stay up when the terminal closes, and its progress must land in a log you can read later.

Before you leave it for the night, practise controlling a foreground job: pause it, see it in the job list, send it to the background, bring it back, and stop it. Then start it again so it keeps writing to `~/batch-export.log` and survives when the terminal closes.

**YOUR TASK:**

1. Run `batch-export` in the foreground. Practise job control: suspend it, list it, resume it in the background and the foreground, then stop it.
2. Start `batch-export` again so it runs in the background, writes stdout and stderr to `~/batch-export.log`, and keeps running when the terminal closes.

**SPEC:**

- Exactly one `batch-export` process is running, as `learner` (not root)
- `~/batch-export.log` exists and keeps growing with `exported batch` lines
- The process survives `kill -HUP <pid>`, which is what a closing terminal sends

**REFERENCES:**

- [DevSetu Blog — Background Jobs: &, jobs, nohup, tmux](/play/devops-engineer/linux/read/background-jobs-and-nohup)

hints: You are learner on a real Ubuntu machine with systemd; sudo works without a password.
Reset gives you a fresh machine (your changes are wiped).
Read SPEC carefully, then Submit — the grader checks the machine itself.

problemStatement.solution:
# Solution — Keep the Batch Running After Logout

When a terminal closes, the kernel sends **SIGHUP** ("hang up") to the processes running in it, and by default they die. `nohup` makes a command ignore SIGHUP. `&` puts it in the background, so you get your prompt back.

Docs: `man nohup` · `man bash` (JOB CONTROL) · `man 7 signal`

## Job control first

```bash
/opt/order-processor/bin/batch-export      # runs in the foreground, holding your prompt
# Ctrl+Z   → stops (suspends) it
jobs        # [1]+  Stopped
bg          # resume it in the background
fg          # bring it back to the foreground
# Ctrl+C   → kill it
```

A background job started this way still dies when the terminal closes.

## Start it properly

```bash
cd ~
nohup /opt/order-processor/bin/batch-export > ~/batch-export.log 2>&1 &
jobs -l
tail -f ~/batch-export.log      # Ctrl+C stops tail, not the batch
```

- `nohup`: ignore SIGHUP.
- `> file 2>&1`: stdout *and* stderr into the log. Without it, nohup writes to `nohup.out`.
- `&`: run in the background.

## Prove it

```bash
pgrep -af batch-export
kill -HUP "$(pgrep -f batch-export)"   # what closing the terminal would do
pgrep -af batch-export                 # still running
```

Then **Submit**. For anything that must survive a reboot as well, use a systemd service (lab 12).
